# What the Eightfold Path Means

*SN 45.8, the Vibhaṅga Sutta — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 3 min · 532 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This page turns the familiar eight-item list into actual instructions. Notice
the progression: understand the problem, aim the heart away from harm, clean
up speech, action, and livelihood, then actively train effort, remembering,
and unification of mind. The final section uses *mental theme* for *jhāna*; here it names
four progressively quieter ways a unified heart is described.

## Translation

### The Noble Eightfold Path

At Sāvatthī, the Buddha said:

"Bhikkhus, I will teach you the noble eightfold path and explain it. Listen and
pay close attention. I will speak."

"Yes, Bhante," the bhikkhus replied.

The Buddha said this:

"And what is the noble eightfold path?

It is:

- right view
- right attitude
- right speech
- right action
- right livelihood
- right effort
- right remembering
- right unification of mind

### Right View

And what is right view?

Knowledge of dissatisfaction, knowledge of its origin, knowledge of its
quenching, and knowledge of how to quench it again.

This is called right view.

### Right Attitude

And what is right attitude?

An attitude of renunciation, an attitude of non-ill-will, and an attitude of
non-harming.

This is called right attitude.

### Right Speech

And what is right speech?

Abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.

This is called right speech.

### Right Action

And what is right action?

Abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual activity.

This is called right action.

### Right Livelihood

And what is right livelihood?

A noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and makes a living by right
livelihood.

This is called right livelihood.

### Right Effort

And what is right effort?

A bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, takes hold of the
heart, and exerts themselves:

- so that unarisen harmful, unwholesome qualities do not arise
- so that arisen harmful, unwholesome qualities are abandoned
- so that unarisen wholesome qualities arise
- so that arisen wholesome qualities remain, do not fade, grow, expand,
  develop, and come to fulfilment

This is called right effort.

### Right Remembering

And what is right remembering?

A bhikkhu remains observing the body in relation to the body—ardent, clearly
knowing, remembering, and with coveting and distress about the world put aside.

They remain observing felt experience in relation to felt experience—ardent,
clearly knowing, remembering, and with coveting and distress about the world
put aside.

They remain observing the heart in relation to the heart—ardent, clearly
knowing, remembering, and with coveting and distress about the world put aside.

They remain observing dhammas among dhammas—ardent, clearly knowing,
remembering, and with coveting and distress about the world put aside.

This is called right remembering.

### Right Unification of Mind

And what is right unification of mind?

A bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensuality and unwholesome qualities, enters
and remains in the first mental theme, with thinking and pondering, and with
rejoicing and satisfaction born of seclusion.

With thinking and pondering subsiding, the heart settles within and becomes
single. They enter and remain in the second mental theme. It is without
thinking and pondering, with rejoicing and satisfaction born of unification.

With the fading of rejoicing, they remain in dynamic balance, remembering and
clearly knowing, and experience satisfaction in the body. They enter and
remain in the third mental theme, of which the noble ones say: 'One of dynamic
balance and remembering stays satisfied.'

With the abandoning of satisfaction and discomfort, and with the earlier
ending of joy and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth mental
theme, without discomfort and without satisfaction, purified by dynamic
balance and remembering.

This is called right unification of mind."

The eighth discourse is finished.

<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>

<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;upekkhā&quot; (often translated &quot;equanimity&quot;) -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.</dd>

<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;citta&quot;: the feeling side of mind. It takes on moods, wants, leans, and reacts. Practice can gladden, steady, train, and release it. Some call it the &quot;heart-mind&quot; or &quot;feeling mind&quot;. Here &quot;heart&quot; does not mean only emotion, or the physical organ.</dd>
<dt><dfn>mental theme</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jhāna&quot; -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble disciple</dfn></dt>
<dd>Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble eightfold path</dfn></dt>
<dd>The eight-part practice these texts teach: right view, right attitude, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right remembering, and right unification of mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>quenching</dfn></dt>
<dd>An extinguishing image for dissatisfaction and its causes going out. Different Pali words use this image on different pages, so the exact scope comes from the sentence.</dd>
<dt><dfn>rejoicing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;pīti&quot; (often translated &quot;rapture&quot;) -- the bright, uplifted gladness that shows up when practice is going well.</dd>
<dt><dfn>remembering</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;sati&quot;. It means actively keeping what matters in mind and coming back to it when you lose it. It is not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right action</dfn></dt>
<dd>Acting without harming -- a factor of the eightfold path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right attitude</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of the path factor usually translated &quot;right intention&quot; -- the underlying motivation a person brings to their actions.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right effort</dfn></dt>
<dd>Effort that is well aimed: heading off what is unhelpful and building up what helps -- a factor of the eightfold path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right livelihood</dfn></dt>
<dd>Making a living in a way that does not depend on harming or deceiving anyone -- a factor of the eightfold path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right remembering</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of the path factor usually translated &quot;right mindfulness&quot; -- keeping what actually matters in view, moment to moment, rather than losing track of it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right speech</dfn></dt>
<dd>Speech that is truthful, kind, timely, and worth saying -- a factor of the eightfold path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right unification of mind</dfn></dt>
<dd>The path factor in which the mind gathers together and becomes unified, supported and directed by the rest of the noble path. The thinking mind and the heart work as one whole; nobody forces them into a trance.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right view</dfn></dt>
<dd>Seeing how experience and practice actually work -- the first factor of the eightfold path. &quot;Right&quot; here means well-aimed and accurate, not morally righteous.</dd>
<dt><dfn>unification</dfn></dt>
<dd>Short for unification of mind (samādhi) inside a longer phrase, such as &quot;born of unification&quot; or &quot;the faculty of unification.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>unwholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;akusala&quot;. Roughly: mentally and ethically harmful. It is blameworthy, leads to harm, and people with good judgment criticize it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>wholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;kusala&quot;. Roughly: mentally and ethically healthy. It is blameless, leads to well-being, and people with good judgment praise it.</dd>
